noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the role of diffusion in gas exchange
understand gas exchange (of carbon dioxide and oxygen) in relation to respiration and photosynthesis

primer.text: Diffusion is the engine of every gas exchange, from an amoeba's membrane to a leaf's stomata. This note starts with the rule itself, then applies it to the plant: which gas crosses where, and how photosynthesis and respiration each set the direction.

lessons.title: Diffusion and Exchange Surfaces
lessons.opening: Particles wander constantly, and diffusion is the net result: movement from where a substance is more concentrated to where it is less so, down the gradient. Single-celled organisms like amoeba manage on their membranes alone; bigger organisms need exchange surfaces — gills, lungs, leaves — built large, thin and, in animals, well ventilated.
keyPoints: Diffusion moves particles from higher to lower concentration, down a gradient.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are the molecules that move this way in gas exchange.
Amoeba exchanges gases straight through its cell membrane.
Multicellular organisms use dedicated exchange surfaces and organ systems.
Effective surfaces share a large area, a thin barrier and steep gradients.

low.restatement: Diffusion is downhill travel for particles, and exchange surfaces make the hill short and wide.
low.analogy: A stadium exit: many wide gates (area) set close to the car park (short distance) empty fastest.
low.examPointer: Quote the three surface features — large, thin, gradient-keeping — for the full mechanism.

medium.restatement: Large, thin and refreshed — the three laws of any exchange surface.
medium.analogy: A motorway works when it has many lanes, short bridges and steady traffic flow.
medium.examPointer: When comparing organisms, always tie a surface feature to faster exchange.

check.stem: Which definition matches diffusion?

options.text: Net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration
options.explanation: That is the gradient-driven movement the specification describes.

options.text: Movement of water across a partially permeable membrane
options.explanation: That is osmosis, water's special case.
Diffusion is passive; energy is not spent.

options.text: Movement of particles against a gradient
options.explanation: Diffusion never runs uphill.

check.stem: How does an amoeba exchange gases?

options.text: By diffusion straight across its cell membrane
options.explanation: A single cell needs no organ; its surface does everything.
Stomata belong to leaves, not amoeba.

options.text: Using lungs inherited from larger cells
options.explanation: Amoeba has no organs at all.
Gas exchange is passive diffusion.

check.stem: What is the gas exchange organ in humans?

options.explanation: Lungs are the human gas exchange organ named here.
Gills belong to fish.
Leaves are the plant's exchange surface.
The heart pumps blood; it exchanges nothing with the air.

check.stem: Which feature of an exchange surface speeds diffusion?

options.explanation: Thin barriers shorten each particle's journey.
Thickness slows exchange; exchange surfaces are thin.
Moisture helps gases dissolve and cross.
Small area reduces the exchange rate.

check.stem: Why do animals ventilate their exchange surfaces?

options.text: To keep the concentration gradients steep for faster exchange
options.explanation: Fresh air or water refreshes the gradient that diffusion feeds on.
Cooling is a separate role; ventilation's exchange job is gradient renewal.

options.text: To filter dust from the air
options.explanation: Filtering is a defensive extra, not the exchange reason.

options.text: Because diffusion would stop without movement
options.explanation: Diffusion slows but does not stop; the point is keeping it fast.

check.stem: Define diffusion in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: Diffusion is the net drift of particles from where they are more concentrated to where they are less so, down a gradient.

check.stem: Name the gas exchange organs of fish, humans and plants.
check.modelAnswer: Fish use gills, humans use lungs, and plants use leaves and roots.

check.stem: Explain why single-celled organisms need no exchange organs.
check.modelAnswer: Because their whole surface touches the environment, so every part of the membrane can exchange directly and the distances involved are tiny; multicellular bodies bury their inner cells, which is why organs become necessary.

check.stem: A spherical cell grows to ten times its diameter. Use surface-area reasoning to predict its gas exchange problem.
check.modelAnswer: Volume grows with the cube of diameter but surface with only the square, so demand for gases far outstrips the membrane able to supply them; diffusion distance to the centre also lengthens, so the cell would suffocate inside unless it found an exchange organ or split.

lessons.title: Gas Exchange in Respiration
lessons.opening: Respiration never pauses, so a plant always consumes oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. At night, with photosynthesis switched off, that consumption is all there is: oxygen diffuses into the leaf down its gradient and carbon dioxide diffuses out, each crossing wherever the leaf lets it.
keyPoints: All living cells respire day and night, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide.
At night no photosynthesis runs, so respiration alone sets the exchange.
Oxygen diffuses into the leaf from the higher concentration outside.
Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the leaf to the lower concentration outside.
Respiring cells keep their internal oxygen low, which maintains the inward gradient.

low.restatement: At night the leaf behaves like any animal tissue: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out.
low.analogy: A shop that only receives deliveries (oxygen) and puts out rubbish (carbon dioxide) after dark.
low.examPointer: Name both directions in your answer — inward oxygen and outward carbon dioxide.

medium.restatement: Respiring cells set the gradients that drive both gas movements.
medium.analogy: A furnace that consumes wood and emits smoke: the difference from the surroundings keeps both flows going.
medium.examPointer: Write the words concentration gradient next to each gas for the mechanism marks.

check.stem: Which gas does a respiring cell consume?

options.explanation: Aerobic respiration takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is the product, not the reactant.
Nitrogen takes no part in respiration.
Water is a product of respiration, not a gas it consumes.

check.stem: At night, which direction does carbon dioxide move in a leaf?

options.text: Out of the leaf, down its gradient
options.explanation: Respiring cells make the inside rich, so the gas leaves.
That would need photosynthesis, which has stopped.
Respiration continues, so the exchange continues.
Gas exchange happens at the leaf's surfaces.

check.stem: Why does oxygen keep diffusing into a respiring leaf all night?

options.text: The respiring cells keep internal oxygen low, so the gradient persists
options.explanation: Constant consumption holds the inside below the outside.

options.text: Because the leaf stores oxygen in vacuoles
options.explanation: Nothing stores oxygen; consumption explains the low level.

options.text: Because the stomata pump air in
options.explanation: Stomata are passive pores; nothing pumps.

options.text: Because oxygen becomes more concentrated inside
options.explanation: Inside stays LOW; that is the whole point.

check.stem: What would happen to gas exchange if a leaf's cells stopped respiring?

options.text: Both gradients would collapse and exchange would cease
options.explanation: No consumption, no low oxygen; no output, no high carbon dioxide.
Without consumption there is no gradient to pull it.

options.text: Only carbon dioxide would still leave
options.explanation: Its gradient depends on respiration too.

options.text: Exchange would continue by active transport
options.explanation: The exchange is passive and gradient-dependent.

check.stem: During the day, which process usually dominates a green leaf's gas exchange?

options.text: Photosynthesis, so the leaf takes in carbon dioxide overall
options.explanation: In sufficient light photosynthesis outruns respiration and reverses the flows.
Respiration runs but is outrun; the net flow favours photosynthesis's pattern.
Both run; photosynthesis simply outpaces.
Transpiration is water loss, not the gas pair's exchange.

check.stem: Name the two gases exchanged during respiration.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen, taken in, and carbon dioxide, released.

check.stem: State the direction of each gas's movement at night.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen enters the leaf while carbon dioxide leaves it.

check.stem: Explain why respiration is described as continuous while photosynthesis is not.
check.modelAnswer: Because every living cell needs energy every moment, and respiration supplies it, whereas photosynthesis depends on light and halts in darkness; the gas exchange of respiration therefore runs around the clock while photosynthesis's runs only in daylight.

check.stem: A sealed jar contains a plant in complete darkness overnight. Predict the air's carbon dioxide level by morning and explain.
check.modelAnswer: The carbon dioxide level rises: with no light the plant only respires, releasing carbon dioxide into the sealed air while consuming its oxygen, and with nowhere for the gas to diffuse the concentration climbs steadily.

lessons.title: Gas Exchange in Photosynthesis
lessons.opening: In daylight the leaf's chemistry flips. Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide, so the inside stays low and the gas is drawn in from the air; oxygen, made as a product, piles up and diffuses out. The gradients are the same tools, pointed the other way.
keyPoints: Photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.
Cells using chloroplasts keep internal carbon dioxide low while photosynthesising.
Carbon dioxide therefore diffuses from outside the leaf inwards.
Oxygen produced inside diffuses outwards, down its own gradient.
Some of the released oxygen is immediately spent by respiration.

low.restatement: Photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide in and pushes oxygen out.
low.analogy: A kitchen cooking with the window open: ingredients come in, steam goes out, both following their own gradients.
low.examPointer: State the direction for both gases and note that respiration still runs underneath.

medium.restatement: The faster process owns the net flow; the slower one trims it.
medium.analogy: Two taps filling and draining one basin: the stronger tap decides whether the level rises or falls.
medium.examPointer: Use the word net when comparing photosynthesis and respiration — examiners look for it.

check.stem: Which gas does photosynthesis consume?

options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is photosynthesis's raw material.
Oxygen is the product; carbon dioxide is consumed.
Nitrogen plays no role here.
Glucose is the sugar made by photosynthesis, not a gas it consumes.

check.stem: During photosynthesis, which way does oxygen move?

options.text: Out of the leaf, down its gradient
options.explanation: Produced inside, oxygen builds up and leaves.
That is respiration's direction at night.

options.text: It stays put inside the chloroplasts
options.explanation: Gas diffuses; some is used by respiration, the rest leaves.

options.text: Through the roots into the soil
options.explanation: Gas exchange happens at the leaf.

check.stem: Why does carbon dioxide keep flowing into a photosynthesising leaf?

options.text: The photosynthesising cells keep internal carbon dioxide low
options.explanation: Constant consumption maintains the inward gradient.

options.text: Because the leaf pumps air inwards
options.explanation: Nothing pumps; diffusion does the work.

options.text: Because carbon dioxide dissolves in the waxy cuticle
options.explanation: The cuticle is a barrier, not an entry route.

options.text: Because the leaf stores it for night
options.explanation: It is consumed immediately, not stored.

check.stem: What happens to the oxygen made during photosynthesis?

options.text: Some is used by respiration and the surplus diffuses out
options.explanation: Respiration runs underneath and spends some of the supply.

options.text: All of it is stored in the vacuole
options.explanation: Nothing stores oxygen; the surplus leaves.
Respiration claims a share first.

options.text: It is converted back into carbon dioxide
options.explanation: That reversal is respiration, not a direct conversion here.

check.stem: When photosynthesis and respiration run at similar rates, what is the net gas exchange?

options.text: Roughly zero — photosynthesis and respiration run at similar rates
options.explanation: Parity between the processes flattens the net flows.
That needs photosynthesis well ahead, which dim light prevents.
That is the darkness outcome.
Both processes still run; only the net shrinks.

check.stem: State the direction of each gas's movement in bright light.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide enters the leaf while oxygen leaves it.

check.stem: Name the organelle where photosynthesis happens.
Explain why a leaf in dim light may show almost no net gas exchange.
check.modelAnswer: Because photosynthesis's consumption of carbon dioxide and release of oxygen nearly match respiration's opposite flows; the two processes cancel almost exactly, so neither gas shows a clear net movement.

check.stem: A greenhouse adds morning light gradually from dark to bright. Describe how the leaf's gas exchange shifts across the morning.
check.modelAnswer: In darkness only respiration runs: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. As light strengthens photosynthesis wakes and trims those flows; near parity the net exchange almost vanishes; in full light photosynthesis dominates and the flows reverse — carbon dioxide in, oxygen out.

glossary.definition: The difference in a substance's level between two regions; diffusion runs down it.
A body surface over which substances enter and leave; large, thin and gradient-keeping when effective.
The overall direction of gas movement after the faster of photosynthesis and respiration has set the balance.
